opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, one of the things that surprised me early on was how much transfer there is. If you do post-training mostly on English data, say instruction-following or a certain style of being helpful, the model will also behave that way when you talk to it in Spanish or Japanese or whatever, even with little or no fine-tuning data in those languages. That tells you something about how these models represent things. The behavioral change isn't stored as "respond this way to English text." It attaches to some more abstract representation of the situation: someone is asking me a question, and I'm supposed to be a helpful assistant answering it.

I think the same phenomenon shows up with modalities, though it's a bit messier there. If you've trained the model to be careful, to admit uncertainty, or to refuse certain kinds of requests in text, a lot of that carries over when the input is an image, as long as the model has a shared enough representation across the two. It's not perfect. You find gaps where the grounding between modalities is weaker, and the behavior doesn't fully transfer. But the default is a surprising amount of generalization.

What I find interesting about this is that it's evidence that post-training mostly isn't teaching the model new knowledge or capabilities. It's more like selecting among behaviors the model already has, choosing which persona or mode it operates in. Once you pick out that persona, it's a fairly global thing, so it shows up everywhere. That cuts both ways. It's great for data efficiency, because you don't need to collect data for every language and every situation. But it also means you can get unintended generalization. If you train on some narrow behavior, it might change the model's overall disposition in ways you didn't expect. So understanding exactly how and why it generalizes matters a lot, both for making these systems useful and for making them behave reliably.

r001.rationale: It says post-training mostly on English instruction-following data makes the model behave similarly when addressed in Spanish or Japanese, even with little or no fine-tuning in those languages.

r002.rationale: It explains that training selects a helpful assistant persona tied to an abstract representation, so that behavior carries across languages.

r003.rationale: It says text-trained carefulness, uncertainty, and refusal behavior often carry over to image inputs in multimodal models, though imperfectly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things that surprised me the most when we were doing RLHF on these models. The intuition going in was that you're teaching the model a behavior, and behaviors are pretty specific, so you'd expect you'd have to cover the space. If you want it to be a good assistant in Spanish, you'd think you need a bunch of Spanish data in your fine-tuning set. And that turned out to be mostly wrong. You can do your instruction tuning and your RL almost entirely in English, and the model will follow instructions in other languages, including languages where you've basically given it zero examples of the assistant persona.

The way I think about it is that pretraining has already given you this huge entangled representation where concepts are shared across languages. The model knows what "being helpful" or "refusing politely" or "writing a numbered list" is as an abstract thing, and the language is almost a surface feature on top. So when you do post-training, you're not really teaching it a skill, you're more selecting a persona or a mode out of the distribution it already has. And personas generalize. You're nudging a fairly small number of degrees of freedom relative to the size of the model, and those degrees of freedom are language-agnostic because of how the pretraining data is structured.

There's a nice piece of evidence for that, which is how little data it takes. Even in the early InstructGPT days, we were seeing that a tiny amount of demonstration data would change the model's behavior broadly. If you were really teaching it something new, that would be very sample-inefficient. The fact that it isn't tells you the capability was mostly there and you're just pointing at it.

The modality case is similar but a bit more subtle. If you have a model that's been trained on text and images jointly, and then you do all your safety or helpfulness training on text, you often get a lot of transfer to the image inputs for free. The model will refuse things or be careful about things in a picture the same way it would in text. But it's not perfect, and the failures are actually really informative. You'll find places where the behavior you trained didn't carry over, and that usually means the representation isn't as shared as you thought. Maybe the image pathway is funneling into the language model in a way that bypasses some of what you shaped. So the generalization gaps become a diagnostic for how unified the model's internal concepts actually are.

The thing I find most interesting about it, honestly, is what it says about what post-training even is. I used to think of it as the stage where you add capabilities. I now think of it much more as the stage where you shape the model's self-concept, and self-concept is the kind of thing that naturally applies everywhere. If the model has decided "I'm the kind of entity that is honest and tries to be useful," that's going to show up whether you talk to it in Japanese or hand it a spreadsheet. Which is encouraging, because it means you don't have to anticipate every context. But it also means that if you get something subtly wrong in that self-concept, it also generalizes everywhere, including to places you weren't testing. So the generalization is a double-edged thing. It's what makes alignment tractable at all, and it's also why small mistakes in the training data can have surprisingly broad effects.

r001.rationale: The response says instruction tuning and RL done almost entirely in English can still produce instruction-following behavior in other languages, even with essentially no examples of the assistant persona in those languages.

r002.rationale: It explains that post-training selects or shapes a helpful assistant persona, and says that persona generalizes across languages because it is language-agnostic.

r003.rationale: It says safety or helpfulness training done on text often transfers to image inputs in jointly trained text-and-image models, including refusing or handling image content carefully.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that post-training seems to change something more general than the particular behavior you’re training on. You might train a model to follow instructions or answer questions better in English, and then see improvements in other languages, even though those languages weren’t represented much in the post-training data.

One way to think about that is that pretraining has already built up the underlying capabilities, and post-training is teaching the model how to use them. It doesn’t have to learn separately, in every language, what it means to give a helpful answer. There’s some shared structure that lets that behavior transfer.

The same question comes up across modalities. If you improve a model’s reasoning using text, does it become better at reasoning about an image? You could imagine the visual part getting the information into a representation that the rest of the model can work with, and then the improvements carrying over. But I wouldn’t expect that transfer to be perfect.

That’s the interesting distinction: when are you teaching a general strategy that can be applied wherever the model already has the relevant capabilities, and when are you teaching something specific to the language or modality? The pattern of what transfers and what doesn’t can tell you something about how those capabilities are organized.

r001.rationale: It describes English post-training benefits transferring to other languages, but says those languages were not represented much—not that the data was English-only.

r002.rationale: It explains transfer through shared structure and teaching the model how to use existing capabilities; it does not attribute it to adopting a helpful persona.

r003.rationale: It raises text-trained reasoning transferring to image reasoning as a possibility, but does not clearly state that text-only fine-tuning can produce reasonable behavior on image inputs.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I find interesting is that the capabilities you train and the data you train them on don’t have to line up in the obvious way. You can do a lot of post-training in English and see improvements in other languages. That suggests you’re doing something more general than teaching the model how to answer a particular set of English questions. You’re changing how it uses capabilities it already acquired during pretraining.

There’s a similar question across modalities. If you teach a model to reason better on text problems, does that help when it’s looking at an image? You could imagine that the visual understanding is already there, and what’s missing is taking the right steps with the information. In that case, text training might help. But if it’s failing to perceive some detail in the image, better reasoning won’t necessarily fix that.

So I think the interesting thing is figuring out which parts are shared. How much of post-training is teaching some fairly general behavior—checking your work, following instructions, deciding when to spend more effort—and how much requires experience with the particular language or modality? The transfer gives you a way to probe that, although an improvement by itself doesn’t tell you exactly what mechanism changed.

r001.rationale: It says English post-training can improve performance in other languages, but does not clearly establish that training uses only English data or that the transfer is to appropriate assistant behavior.

r002.rationale: It attributes transfer to changes in how the model uses existing capabilities, not to adopting a helpful persona that carries across languages.

r003.rationale: It raises text-to-image transfer as a question and says text training might help under a condition; it does not clearly state that text-only fine-tuning can generalize to reasonable image-input behavior.
